procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Magistrate extended by the State Government under Section 144(6) of the Criminal Procedure Code.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court set aside the order passed by the Magistrate, viewing that the State Government's extension of the order under Section 144 imposed an unreasonable restriction on fundamental freedoms because it wasn't subject to judicial scrutiny and lacked a mechanism for rescission or alteration.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of Bihar appealed to the Supreme Court. The Union of India intervened. The Supreme Court appointed an amicus curiae and notified the Attorney General because the case concerned central legislation. The Supreme Court ultimately dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision.

decision.appeal_result: In accordance with the opinion of the majority the appeal is dismissed. In the result this appeal fails and the same is dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appeal should be allowed.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal in accordance with the opinion of the majority. One judge expressed a dissenting view, stating that the appeal should have been allowed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appeal should be allowed.
appellant_arguments: Initially, the State argued that the order made by the State Government is an administrative order and therefore not subject to judicial review.

Later, the State changed its position, arguing that the only operative orders were those made by the Magistrate, which the Government merely extended. They contended that the Government's order merged with the Magistrate's orders and that this extended order was open to review and revision under the Criminal Procedure Code.
respondent_arguments: A key test for a reasonable restriction is whether the aggrieved party has a right of representation against it.
No person can be deprived of their liberty without a fair and reasonable opportunity to be heard in their defence.
The court must determine if the restriction is excessive or imposed in an arbitrary manner.
The restriction in question is not a reasonable restriction and is therefore unconstitutional as it violates Article 19.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: To determine if a restriction on a fundamental right is reasonable, courts must examine both the substantive and procedural aspects of the law on a case-by-case basis, considering all attendant circumstances. A restriction is reasonable only if it is not arbitrary or excessive, and the procedure for its imposition is fair and just, which includes affording the aggrieved party an adequate opportunity to be heard or make a representation against it.
obiter: No abstract standard or general pattern of reasonableness can be laid down as applicable to all cases.
The State has not been consistent in its stand.
The scheme of s. 144, Criminal Procedure Code, empowers a magistrate to make an order, provides for review of that order, and lays down the procedure to be adopted.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The power conferred on the State Government by s. 144(6) is an independent executive power, not expected to be exercised judicially, and is open to be exercised arbitrarily. As there is no provision for the aggrieved party to make a representation against the government's direction, no appeal or revision is provided, and the order need not be of a temporary nature, the restriction is not a reasonable restriction. Therefore, the provision is unconstitutional as it is violative of Article 19(1)(b)(c) and (d).
legal_tests_applied: In considering reasonableness of laws imposing restrictions on fundamental rights both substantive and procedural aspects of the law should be examined from the point of view of reasonableness.
In order to be a reasonable restriction, the same must not be arbitrary or excessive and the procedure and the manner of imposition of the restriction must also be fair and just.

One of the important tests to find out whether a restriction is reasonable is to see whether the aggrieved party has a right of representation against the restriction imposed or proposed to be imposed.
The courts have to see whether the restriction is in excess of the requirement or whether it is imposed in an arbitrary manner.
why_appellant_lost: The power conferred on the Government is an independent executive power, not expected to be exercised judicially, and is open to be exercised arbitrarily.
The ambit of the power conferred on the government is very large and is uncontrolled.
The directions given in the exercise of that power need not be of a temporary nature.

The law fails to provide procedural safeguards, as there is no provision to make representation by the aggrieved party against the direction given by the Government, and no appeal or revision is provided against that direction.
why_respondent_won: The impugned restriction is not a reasonable restriction and therefore does not get the protection of Sub-Arts. (3), (4) and (5) of Art. 19.
The restriction fails the test of procedural reasonableness because the aggrieved party has no right of representation against the government's order.
The restriction is substantively unreasonable because the power is conferred on the executive government, not a judicial authority, and the order made need not be of a temporary nature.
policy_considerations: Any restriction which is opposed to the fundamental principles of liberty and justice cannot be considered reasonable.
No person can be deprived of his liberty without being afforded an opportunity to be heard in defence and that opportunity must be adequate, fair and reasonable.

Since the making of an order under s. 144 involves serious infringement of the rights of the citizens, exercise of the power should be conditioned by a judicial evaluation of the circumstances which necessitate it.
